query: For a selected high-entropy alloy whose superconducting behavior remains uncharacterized, what governs whether and how superconductivity emerges in the low-temperature test regime, and why? Propose one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison with the starting state, the observations expected relative to that baseline, the limits over which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the selected high‐entropy alloy (HEA), superconductivity emerges at low temperatures because the chemically complex but homogeneously disordered bcc structure enhances electron–phonon coupling. This robust coupling facilitates Cooper pair formation despite the high degree of atomic randomness.
generation.material_initial_state: The as-cast HEA in a homogeneous bcc phase with a nearly uniform distribution of several constituent elements.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sample sets: one with full high configurational entropy (i.e., multiple principal elements) and one control alloy whose composition is simplified (thus lower entropy) by reducing the number of elements while keeping similar average atomic concentrations. Test both under identical low-temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at low temperatures (typically below 10 K) under ambient pressure (with potential extension to high pressure) where the bcc phase is stable.
generation.structural_mediator: The stabilized bcc crystal lattice that, despite atomic disorder, provides a uniform background, allowing localized lattice softening and enhanced phonon modes.
generation.mechanism: The high degree of atomic randomness in the HEA minimizes phase separation and local lattice distortions that would normally scatter electrons. Instead, this disorder promotes a uniform electron–phonon interaction environment which increases the density of effective phonon modes. These modes boost the electron–phonon coupling strength and lead to Cooper pair formation at a critical temperature similar to other type-II HEA superconductors.
generation.predicted_outcome: The high-entropy sample will exhibit a superconducting transition (Tc in the range of about 7–8 K) along with robust type-II behavior (evidenced by a high upper critical field). In contrast, the lower-entropy control sample is predicted to show a reduced Tc or even an absence of superconductivity if the electron–phonon coupling is insufficiently enhanced.
generation.baseline: The superconducting properties measured for the lower-entropy (simpler composition) alloy serve as the baseline against which the high-entropy sample's enhanced superconductivity is compared.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEAs that stabilize in a homogeneous bcc phase with similar alloying ratios to those in previously studied systems (e.g., (TaNb)_0.67(HfZrTi)_0.33). The effect might be limited if excessive disorder or additional factors (e.g., significantly altered carrier concentrations) override the benefits of enhanced electron–phonon coupling.
generation.uncertainty: While there is evidence from similar HEAs showing robust superconductivity, the precise influence of configurational entropy on the electron–phonon coupling strength and its interplay with potential defect or carrier density effects remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloy samples: one maintaining high configurational entropy (multiple principal elements in a homogeneous bcc phase) and one modified to have reduced entropy (fewer alloying elements, but similar average composition). Perform systematic low-temperature electrical resistance and magnetization measurements to determine the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and critical fields (Hc1, Hc2). Parallel structural characterization (e.g., X-ray diffraction, EDXS) will ensure that both types of samples maintain comparable crystal structures.
measurements: Temperature-dependent electrical resistance to determine Tc
Magnetization measurements (e.g., SQUID) for critical field determination
Structural analysis (XRD, EDXS) to verify homogeneous bcc phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy alloy does not exhibit a significantly enhanced Tc or superior type-II superconducting characteristics (e.g., higher Hc2) compared to the reduced-entropy control sample, or if it fails to superconduct at all, then the hypothesized mechanism that high configurational entropy enhances electron–phonon coupling (and thereby drives superconductivity) is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The formation and physical properties of a novel high-entropy alloy Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 are presented and described. As expected for type-A HEA superconductors, the alloy crystallizes in a simple bcc structure. At the same time, a compositional analysis by EDXS shows a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements in the studied sample. The determined physical properties indicate that the alloy exhibits type II superconductivity with a conventional type II superconductor with a critical temperature Tc close to 7.5 K, an intermediate electron–phonon coupling and an upper critical field μ0Hc2=12.2(1) T. This significant finding indicates that Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 has one of the highest μ0Hc2 in the family of type-A HEA superconductors.

Pressure is one of the variables that can uncover unexpected phenomena and properties (). For superconductors in particular, the pressure-induced enhancement of critical transition temperatures in copper-oxide and iron-pnictide superconductors (), the reemergence of superconductivity in the alkaline iron selenide () and heavy fermion superconductors (), pressure-induced superconductivity in H3S () and elements (, ), are examples. Therefore, looking for new phenomena in the superconducting HEA under pressure is of great interest. Here we report high-pressure studies on the superconducting HEA (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33, which has a critical transition temperature to the superconducting state (TC) of about 7.8 K at ambient pressure (, ). Our observations demonstrate that this alloy exhibits extraordinarily robust superconductivity––its zero-resistance superconducting state is still achieved even at a pressure of 190.6 GPa, or almost 2 megabars (1 Mbar = 1011 pascal), a pressure like that within the outer core of the earth. Such a superconductor with a highly robust zero-resistance state, existing continuously from 1 atm to geological pressures, is extremely unusual and is in fact unique

Superconductivity Under Pressure. Fig. 1A shows the temperature dependence of the electrical resistance at ambient pressure for a (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 sample. A sharp drop to a zero-resistance superconducting state is observed at ∼7.7 K (we define TC as the temperature where the resistance changes from a finite value to zero), consistent with the results reported in ref. . Applying a magnetic field on the sample shows that its superconducting transition temperature (TC) systematically shifts to lower temperature (Fig. 1A, Inset), as expected. Temperature-dependent constant-current magnetic susceptibility characterization was also performed for the ambient-pressure sample. As shown in Fig. 1B, a strong diamagnetic response is observed starting at 7.6 K, indicative of a bulk superconducting nature. High-pressure resistance measurements were performed for four samples that were cut from the material used as the standard for the superconductivity at ambient pressure. The electrical resistance measurements for these samples were performed between 4 and 300 K.
